r.t: Late one night in your wooden house, you hear a knock at the front door: three slow knocks. You live alone, in the middle of nowhere, and the door you built faces only forest. Through the spruce planks you hear a thin, polite voice saying, 'Knock knock.' The torch beside the door flickers, and the door seems to be waiting for you to answer.
r.b: Creep to the window and look outside
r.c: Stay silent and stack furniture against the door

ra.t: 'Who's there?' you call. 'Door,' says the voice, pleased. 'Door who?' you hear yourself ask. 'Doorway,' it whispers, 'to somewhere else.' The latch begins to rattle, and the door slowly starts to push inward on its own, letting in a thread of cold air that smells like old rain and nails.
ra.a: Hold the door shut with your shoulder
ra.b: Step back and let it open
ra.c: Draw your sword and shout 'Show yourself!'

rb.t: You creep to the window and wipe the frost from the glass. Outside, the snow is untouched, no footprints at all, except one trail that starts at your door and walks away into the forest, step by slow step. The knocking, you realize, is coming from the inside of your own door. In the reflection on the glass, the door behind you has just opened a crack.
rb.a: Turn around and face the door
rb.b: Smash the window and climb out

rc.t: You drag the chest, the bed, and the furnace in front of the door and sit panting on the floor. The knocking stops. Then it starts again from the walls, left, right, above, below, circling the house like a slow heartbeat. The voice now whispers from inside the walls themselves: 'Knock knock. Who's home?'

raa.t: You throw your shoulder against the door as it pushes inward. Something on the other side pushes back with the same strength, patient and calm, and the wood groans. The voice says, 'You built me to open. Why do you keep me closed?' You realize the hinges are your own work, and every nail in the frame feels warm.
raa.a: Tell it you're sorry and open it
raa.b: Brace the door with an iron block

rab.t: You step back. The door opens slowly and silently onto a hallway that is not your porch. A long corridor of identical doors stretches into the dark, each with a faint light under it, and each one softly knocking. The voice says, 'Come in, come in,' and the floor under your feet becomes cool, smooth stone.

rac.t: 'Show yourself!' you shout. The knocking stops. Slowly the door swings open, and no one is there, only the empty doorway and the night forest. Then the shadow of the doorframe stretches across the floor toward you and stands up, taking the shape of a tall man with no face. It tilts its head like a polite guest waiting to be invited in.
rac.c: Light a torch at its feet

rba.t: You turn around. The door is closed, the bolt still in place, but the knocking keeps going, soft and rhythmic, from the inside surface of the wood. Three knocks, then a whisper: 'Please let me out.' Not in. Out. Something is trapped inside your door.
rba.a: Unbolt it and open the door
rba.c: Take the door off its hinges

rbb.t: Glass explodes into the snow, and you tumble out into the freezing night. You follow the single line of footprints, because it is the only direction that isn't your house. The prints lead to a small clearing where a second door stands alone among the trees, slightly open, glowing warmly from inside. The knocking has stopped.
rbb.b: Close the door and lock it with a stone

rbc.t: In the glass, the door creeps open an inch at a time. A pale hand with long fingers grips the frame from the outside. You can't make yourself turn around. In the reflection, just behind your shoulder, a face leans into the room, smiling politely. It looks exactly like you did as a child.

rca.t: Under the bed it is dusty and cramped. The knocking stops directly above you, and the floorboards creak as someone gently sits on the mattress, humming a tune. A cold hand slowly lowers over the edge of the mattress, palm open, and waits.
rca.c: Slide out the other side and run

rcb.t: You climb into the attic and pull the ladder up behind you. The knocking follows you, tapping along the beams, patient and slow. Among the dusty chests you find an old lantern and a tall mirror leaning against the rafters. In the mirror, you notice, the attic has a door that the real attic does not.
rcb.a: Open the door in the mirror
rcb.b: Cover the mirror with a sheet

rcc.t: You knock three times on the wall, slowly. The circling stops. After a long silence, three knocks answer, soft and slow, right where your hand is resting. A tiny door-shaped crack appears in the plaster, glowing faintly gold, and a small, cheerful voice says, 'At last, somebody who knocks back!'
rcc.b: Knock out a rhythm, like a code

raaa.t: You apologize and swing the door wide. Moonlight pours in, and the shape that stood there, tall as the frame and made of grain and nails, bows politely and steps inside. It only wanted to see the house it was built for. It walks every room, touching each wall with gratitude, then returns to its frame, and from that night your door opens for you gently, without a sound.

raab.t: You brace the door with an iron block, and the pushing stops. The voice sighs. All night long, something drags its fingers down the outside of the wall, slow and sad. In the morning the door is covered in scratches that spell one word, again and again: OPEN. You never use the front door again, and the house feels smaller every day.

raac.t: You squint through the keyhole. An enormous eye stares back, golden and ancient, filling the hole completely. It blinks. The door swings open in a rush of cold air, and you realize you are standing on the doorstep while your house, your lantern light, and the whole forest are inside the eye. When you look back, the door is just a door, and you are standing at someone else's house.

raba.t: You walk in, and the doors fall silent as you pass, one after another, as if holding their breath. At the very end is a door with your name carved on it. You open it, and it is your bedroom, warm and safe, and the corridor behind you is gone. Somewhere a door sighs with relief, and you realize you have been tucked in by something very old.

rabb.t: You slam the door. The corridor is gone, and the voice is laughing now, deep and amused, from every wall. The door begins to knock from the inside, and the sound is coming from the room right behind you. When you turn around, the door that was behind you now has a keyhole, and a pale eye pressed to it, watching.

rabc.t: You knock on the nearest door. It opens an inch, and a tiny hand slides out holding a small brass key. A whisper tells you this key opens the way out, but only if you promise to leave one thing behind. You promise, and the key turns, and you step out onto your porch at dawn without your shadow.

raca.t: Your sword goes through the shadow like cold water. It laughs softly and wraps around you like a coat. You stand in your own house, wearing a shadow that is slightly too big, and from then on you knock before you enter every door, because you never know what is waiting on the other side.

racb.t: You pull up a chair, and the shadow sits, hat in hand, as though used to being invited. It says it has stood outside every door in the world, waiting for someone to ask it in. You talk until sunrise, and when the light comes it thanks you and folds itself into a doormat that reads WELCOME, which stays there for years.

racc.t: The torch flares at its feet, and the shadow shrieks like tearing cloth, tearing itself in half, then in quarters, every piece scattering across the walls. The house goes silent. In the morning every shadow in the house falls the wrong way, and your own points slightly toward the door.

rbaa.t: You unbolt the door, and a small gray moth made of wood shavings flutters out and settles on your sleeve. It had been sealed in the frame when the door was built, long ago, and it only wanted the sky. It flies out into the dawn, your door never creaks again, and in spring a tiny sapling grows beside the porch.

rbab.t: 'I'm the tree you cut down,' says the voice from the grain. It tells you of its roots, the wind, and the birds that nested in its branches, and you listen in the dark. At sunrise you plant a sapling beside the door, and the knocking stops, and every morning the door smells faintly of rain and pine.

rbac.t: You lift the door off its hinges and lean it against the wall. Behind it there is no wall, only a night forest stretching in every direction, and a thousand doors standing among the trees, each one knocking, each one waiting. You hang the door back up with shaking hands and decide to sleep with the lights on for the rest of your life.

rbba.t: You step through, and the door closes softly behind you. Inside is your own house, perfectly warm, every torch lit, a table set for two. A tall quiet figure sits in the far chair and says, 'Finally.' You sit down, because there is nothing else to do, and you have supper with something that has been waiting patiently for years to be invited.

rbbb.t: You drag a stone across the door and stack another on top. The glow dies, and a long low sigh rolls through the forest like wind leaving a lung. You walk home through the dark, and your front door is exactly as you left it, unlocked and quiet. From then on you leave a candle in the window, just in case something else is out there.

rbbc.t: You run back and climb in through the broken window, and your house feels warm and ordinary. You pull the blanket over your head and fall asleep. In the morning the window is whole again, the snow outside is unmarked, and a single small knock sounds at the glass, gentle and cheerful, like a bird.

rbca.t: You say your name. The face pauses, tilts its head, and says it back, exactly the way your mother used to. It steps into the room, and you realize it only came to give you a message. It tells you to forgive someone, and you know exactly who. When you open your eyes, the door is closed, and your hands are wet with tears you didn't notice.

rbcb.t: You close your eyes, and the house goes completely silent. A long time passes. When you finally look, it is morning and the door is bolted, but small muddy footprints lead from the door to your bed and back out to the snow. Beside your pillow lies a single wooden toy, and you do not remember ever owning it.

rbcc.t: You smile back. The face's smile widens, then widens again, past where a smile should stop, and the room tilts. The door bursts open, and a wind of old laughter carries it out into the night, taking your smile with it. For a week you can't smile, and when you finally do, it feels like a borrowed one.

rcaa.t: You take the hand. It is dry and light, like old paper, and it squeezes yours once, kindly. A voice says, 'Now you're not alone,' and the humming becomes a lullaby. You fall asleep under the bed, safe, and wake at noon in a room that is warmer than it ever was before. The door is open, and the forest outside is bright.

rcab.t: You stay perfectly still, holding your breath. The hand waits, then withdraws. The mattress rises as the weight lifts, and the footsteps cross the room and stop at the door. It knocks twice, politely, like a guest leaving, and walks away. You stay under the bed until the sun comes up, and you never fully trust furniture again.

rcac.t: You slide out and bolt for the window. Behind you the whole bed is empty, and the humming turns into laughter. You dive into the snow, and the house door slams open and shut, again and again, as if applauding. You run until you reach a village, and for the rest of the night every door you pass knocks softly as you go by.

rcba.t: You reach through the mirror and open the door. Beyond it you see your house exactly as it is, but with every light on and a family sitting at the table: you, older, and people you love. They look up and smile. You step through, and the door closes, and the attic is empty. People say that house is haunted now, but kindly.

rcbb.t: You throw the sheet over the mirror. The knocking stops at once. In the quiet you hear the sheet breathe, in and out, as if something behind it is sleeping. You tiptoe down the ladder, leave the house forever, and never find out what was in the mirror. Years later you still avoid looking at covered furniture.

rcbc.t: The mirror shatters, and each shard shows a door, each door slightly open. A hundred voices whisper 'Knock knock' at once, and the house trembles. You tumble down the ladder and out the front door, which opens without a sound. When you look back, the house is dark, and a hundred tiny doors are glowing in its windows.

rcca.t: You open the little door. Inside is a miniature room, no bigger than a cupboard, with a tiny table, tiny lamps, and a very old, very small gentleman in a nightcap. He explains that he is the spirit of the house, and that nobody had said hello since the builders. He gives you a tiny key to the front door, and from then on the house always keeps you warm.

rccb.t: You tap out a rhythm, and the walls answer with a perfect echo, then add a beat of their own. Soon the whole house is drumming, floorboards, rafters, windows, and doors, a joyful midnight song that only you can hear. By morning the house is warmer than it has ever been, and every door in it opens on the first try.

rccc.t: 'Who's there?' you whisper. A long pause. Then the voice says, softly, 'You are.' The crack in the wall widens, and you see yourself standing in your own kitchen from outside, looking in through the tiny door. You have been the one knocking all along, and the house, gently and politely, lets you back in.
